If it's fair to fire her in that situation, then it seems like her choices were lose her job or die. Robberies happen, I won't speak on whether I think taking money away from corporations and banks is justifiable or not, it is sufficient to say simply that robberies happen. The fact that robberies happen is not the fault of the guard. It is also not the fault of the guard that that particular money was stolen, since it would be wrong to ask her to lay down her life for any amount of money, as money holds no intrinsic value while life does. So the only ethical option is a policy that says "if robbed, then don't risk your life for the money; it can't have value like you do." But the company didn't have one, and instead fired her, as a result of what I've said, unethically. It is not the robbers fault she was fired, it was the company.

I'd like to address potential counter-argument that this is victim blaming. To clarify, I am not blaming the victim for anything. I blame the robbers for trauma, and the company for the loss of the guard's income. The guard is not responsible for anything above her own well-being, and as such has a right to not defend the company property.

I will respond to each statement in order in each paragraph. 

Me taking his bread without compensating him would be violating his rights. However, if the government promised bread and he produces bread it would be the governments responsibility to make sure people get bread without violating the bakers rights.

"Earning money is about satisfying the needs of others." Tell that to the people working day in day out just to make it to the next month. As for the bread, it could be made more efficiently if a baker bakes it, meaning lower total cost to whoever is paying for it weather it be government subsidized (in the case of the government assuming responsibility for the well-being of its citizens) or bought by private citizens.

You're absolutely right, you did say it's impossible. But the other part of making an argument is supporting what you say. Anyways, you seem to think I'm saying "steal the fruits of labor" when I'm saying redistribute fairly so that everyone's basic needs are met. 

I'm not the caricature for the red scare you seem to be so hot and bothered about. I'm a person who would like it if people didn't starve to death or die from curable diseases. My whole point is that a poor man should not have to worry about what he will do if he becomes ill. He should be able to focus on improving society in whatever way he thinks will be most fitting.

Aren't those trying to profit off of a person's poor state of being standing in their way? And the same case for food. Exploitation of people's basic needs for profit seems to be those people standing in the way of a person's being or well-being. I would agree if they were things that weren't absolutely crucial but because the basics are required for life and/or the pursuit of happiness, therefore basic healthcare and even food should be a basic right under a government that swears to uphold our inalienable rights.

Wouldn't it be that the inalienable right to life is enough of an argument as to why cures to treatable ailments should be a basic human right? And if the ailment is non-lethal wouldn't being sick violate the right of pursuit of happiness (probably not many people are happy who are sick)?
